thread.title: Tesla's Biggest Bull Says Its Factory 'Mess' Is a Sign of Good Things to Come

title: Tesla's Biggest Bull Says Its Factory 'Mess' Is a Sign of Good Things to Come
text:
Tesla’s Biggest Bull Says Its Factory ‘Mess’ Is a Sign of Good Things to Come By Updated Dec. 5, 2018 11:09 a.m. ET Order Reprints Photograph by Jasper Juinen/Bloomberg Text size
Tesla ’s biggest bull recently visited the company’s factory in Fremont, Calif., coming away with the opinion that the facility is a “crowded mess” jammed with “unnecessary complexity”—all of which is good news for investors.
Pierre Ferragu, of New Street Research, wrote Tuesday that a conveyor belt meant to bring parts to the assembly line had been scrapped and replaced with manual delivery, contributing to production lines “30% less productive than initially anticipated.”
“All this feeds a lot of bear argument on the company,” said Ferragu, whose $530 price target on Tesla (ticker: TSLA) shares is the highest on Wall Street—more than 60% above the average—according to FactSet. “We see it the exact opposite way. Failure is where one learns the most.” Short selling offers the opportunity to make money on a falling stock. But the potential for loss is unlimited.
The argument, Ferragu wrote, is that as Tesla seeks to boost production, things can only get better. (Yes, that phrase was indeed inserted as an excuse to link to a Howard Jones video .)
“By shooting way too high, Tesla failed on its original plan, but achieved a world class result,” Ferragu wrote. “The next production sites will be much more efficient, and will ramp very rapidly.”
Shares of Tesla, up more than 15% in 2018, have risen nearly 36% in the fourth quarter so far. They closed Tuesday around $350.
Last week was packed with Tesla news. Among stories Barron’s covered: Elon Musk said the company nearly died as it fired up Model 3 production, and recent Chinese sales were reportedly slow (though the company took swift aim at the latter report).
And the week ended with reports that the company had managed to make 1,000 Model 3 sedans in a day . That rate, if it becomes stable, would represent substantial growth in output from the end of the third quarter. That, Ferragu wrote, doesn’t seem like a tremendous leap. (Tuesday, meanwhile, Barron’s covered a bank’s “outrageous” prediction that Apple (AAPL) would buy Tesla in 2019.) Newsletter Sign-up
“The road to 7,000 units per week seems easy, and limited capital expenditures will be required (in the low tens of millions) to get to 10,000,” he wrote. (Musk hasn’t discussed a specific long-term Model 3 production goal, but 10,000 is in line with theoretical demand numbers he has mentioned.)
“We don’t know for sure what demand will ultimately be, but we know that from here, Tesla will expand its price range, introduce leasing, and expand internationally,” Ferragu wrote. “ All these levers combined have a lot of depth and should be more than enough to get to 10,000 Model 3 per week at the end of next year.”
